hits.text:
i can’t comprehend why people explain their codebase to Opus again every single morning

Claude Code already has memory.

most people just never run it as a system:

→ write: Opus saves every correction and decision as its own topic file

→ consolidate: an Opus subagent merges, dedupes and prunes them

→ recall: MEMORY.md loads at startup, topic files only when needed

→ the index stays short so nothing gets cut off

Opus remembers. You stop repeating yourself.

paste this into claude code 👇

~/.claude/agents/consolidator.md

---
name: consolidator
description: consolidates auto memory. merges duplicates, prunes stale entries, keeps MEMORY.md a short index.
model: opus
tools: Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep
---
You maintain this project's auto memory directory.
1. Read MEMORY.md and every topic file.
2. Merge duplicates into one file. Delete facts that are stale or contradicted by newer ones.
3. Rewrite MEMORY.md as an index: one line per memory, linking its topic file.
4. Keep MEMORY.md under 150 lines. Detail lives in topic files, never in the index.
5. Return a short list of what you merged, deleted and kept.
Set up a write, consolidate, recall memory system for this project.
1. Make sure auto memory is on: "autoMemoryEnabled": true in ~/.claude/settings.json. Keep everything else in that file.
2. Create ~/.claude/agents/consolidator.md from the block above.
3. Add to CLAUDE.md: "When I correct you or we make a decision, save it to auto memory as its own topic file. At the end of a long session, run the consolidator agent."
Show me the diff before changing anything.

"No indication Ledger's systems were compromised."

Technically true.

But someone still opened Ledger devices, planted a spy chip, resealed the box, and sold them through a reseller Ledger worked with.

The chip sat on the screen's data lines and copied the 24 words during setup.

The secure element can't protect a seed phrase that gets read straight off the display.

And the packaging looked untouched.

So the real questions:

Who was checking this reseller?

Why could a tampered device pass as new?

Why are anti tampering solutions only coming now, after an estimated $86M is gone?

The tech wasn't broken.

The supply chain was.

And for users, that's the same thing.

virals.name: Aakash Gupta
virals.text:
Mark Zuckerberg was about to spend up to $200 billion, more than the entire Disney company is worth, on an AI that didn't exist yet. So he asked the guy building it if he was sure it would work, and even that guy wasn't sure.

The guy is Alexandr Wang, who runs Meta's AI lab, and the story came out on John Collison's podcast this week. Late last year Meta's top executives were together in Hawaii, and Wang says the CFO, Susan Li, pulled him aside more than once on that trip to warn him that if the model flopped, it would be really, really bad for Meta's finances. All he could show her was his gut read on how the research was going and a few charts.

She had every reason to be nervous. Meta spent $72 billion on capex in 2025, and the plan for 2026 now runs $130 to $145 billion. Last quarter, free cash flow at one of the most profitable companies on the planet fell to $784 million, and Meta borrowed about $25 billion in the bond market in the same stretch.

So why not wait until you know it works?

Because in AI you have to pour the concrete years before you find out what it's for. Meta started planning its two giant clusters, Prometheus in Ohio and the 5 gigawatt Hyperion in Louisiana, back in 2023 and 2024. That was before Llama 4 disappointed, and before Wang ever got the WhatsApp message from Zuck asking if he had time for a call. Meta was building the biggest computers in its history for an AI lab that didn't exist yet.

Wang called the whole thing the opposite of Lean Startup, where you test something small and only spend real money once it works. Muse Wonder got planned in August of last year and shipped this Monday, and the biggest checks were signed with the answer still most of a year away.

What makes it even more nerve-wracking is how few people the bet rides on. Zuck says the research team is under 200 people, closer to 100, with infrastructure staff on top. Run his own numbers and every researcher in that lab is carrying something like a billion dollars of Meta's money.

When John Collison asked whether Meta will actually make money from any of this, Zuck's first answer was "The answer better be yes." A second later he corrected himself and just said yes.

virals.name: Aakash Gupta
virals.text:
A company had an AI interview a guy for a job, so he had his own AI clone sit in for him and walked out of the room.

Which means there's a job interview going on right now with zero people in it. And honestly, he made the most rational move of anybody involved. An economist basically called it back in 1973.

His name was Michael Spence, and he won a Nobel Prize for this idea. Companies can't see inside your head to know if you're any good, so they look at stuff that's a pain for you to produce. You spend four years getting a degree, or you sit on a live call for an hour where you can't hide anything. The hassle is the whole point. Somebody who isn't serious about the job won't put up with it, and that's how the company sorts real candidates from everyone else.

Problem is, AI has been making that stuff easy to fake. Cover letters went first, then résumés. Gartner surveyed 3,000 job seekers and 6% admitted to some kind of interview fraud, like having someone else pretend to be them. Researchers at Palo Alto Networks showed a person with zero editing experience could build a fake candidate good enough to get through a video interview in about 70 minutes.

That left the live interview as pretty much the last thing that still took real effort from you. Then companies decided their own side of it wasn't worth a recruiter's time and started sending avatars.

Put yourself in his shoes for a second. The company wouldn't spend one minute of a human's time on him, but still expected him to sit there and perform for software that turns him into a score. If they're not going to show up, why would he? The company was the first one to skip its own interview, and all he did was return the favor.

So you've got two AIs trading polished answers while his camera films an empty room, and nobody comes out of it knowing anything. The company has no clue if he can actually do the job, and he has no clue if the job is even real. Gartner found only about half of job seekers believe the postings they apply to are legit in the first place.

I'd bet the fix ends up looking pretty old school. Gartner also found 62% of candidates are more likely to apply when a job requires an in-person interview, so the serious ones are already telling companies they'd rather just show up. A lot of companies paid good money to automate the handshake, and they're about to pay again to bring it back.

outsiders.name: Aakash Gupta
outsiders.text:
Mark Zuckerberg was about to spend up to $200 billion, more than the entire Disney company is worth, on an AI that didn't exist yet. So he asked the guy building it if he was sure it would work, and even that guy wasn't sure.

The guy is Alexandr Wang, who runs Meta's AI lab, and the story came out on John Collison's podcast this week. Late last year Meta's top executives were together in Hawaii, and Wang says the CFO, Susan Li, pulled him aside more than once on that trip to warn him that if the model flopped, it would be really, really bad for Meta's finances. All he could show her was his gut read on how the research was going and a few charts.

She had every reason to be nervous. Meta spent $72 billion on capex in 2025, and the plan for 2026 now runs $130 to $145 billion. Last quarter, free cash flow at one of the most profitable companies on the planet fell to $784 million, and Meta borrowed about $25 billion in the bond market in the same stretch.

So why not wait until you know it works?

Because in AI you have to pour the concrete years before you find out what it's for. Meta started planning its two giant clusters, Prometheus in Ohio and the 5 gigawatt Hyperion in Louisiana, back in 2023 and 2024. That was before Llama 4 disappointed, and before Wang ever got the WhatsApp message from Zuck asking if he had time for a call. Meta was building the biggest computers in its history for an AI lab that didn't exist yet.

Wang called the whole thing the opposite of Lean Startup, where you test something small and only spend real money once it works. Muse Wonder got planned in August of last year and shipped this Monday, and the biggest checks were signed with the answer still most of a year away.

What makes it even more nerve-wracking is how few people the bet rides on. Zuck says the research team is under 200 people, closer to 100, with infrastructure staff on top. Run his own numbers and every researcher in that lab is carrying something like a billion dollars of Meta's money.

When John Collison asked whether Meta will actually make money from any of this, Zuck's first answer was "The answer better be yes." A second later he corrected himself and just said yes.

outsiders.name: Aakash Gupta
outsiders.text:
A company had an AI interview a guy for a job, so he had his own AI clone sit in for him and walked out of the room.

Which means there's a job interview going on right now with zero people in it. And honestly, he made the most rational move of anybody involved. An economist basically called it back in 1973.

His name was Michael Spence, and he won a Nobel Prize for this idea. Companies can't see inside your head to know if you're any good, so they look at stuff that's a pain for you to produce. You spend four years getting a degree, or you sit on a live call for an hour where you can't hide anything. The hassle is the whole point. Somebody who isn't serious about the job won't put up with it, and that's how the company sorts real candidates from everyone else.

Problem is, AI has been making that stuff easy to fake. Cover letters went first, then résumés. Gartner surveyed 3,000 job seekers and 6% admitted to some kind of interview fraud, like having someone else pretend to be them. Researchers at Palo Alto Networks showed a person with zero editing experience could build a fake candidate good enough to get through a video interview in about 70 minutes.

That left the live interview as pretty much the last thing that still took real effort from you. Then companies decided their own side of it wasn't worth a recruiter's time and started sending avatars.

Put yourself in his shoes for a second. The company wouldn't spend one minute of a human's time on him, but still expected him to sit there and perform for software that turns him into a score. If they're not going to show up, why would he? The company was the first one to skip its own interview, and all he did was return the favor.

So you've got two AIs trading polished answers while his camera films an empty room, and nobody comes out of it knowing anything. The company has no clue if he can actually do the job, and he has no clue if the job is even real. Gartner found only about half of job seekers believe the postings they apply to are legit in the first place.

I'd bet the fix ends up looking pretty old school. Gartner also found 62% of candidates are more likely to apply when a job requires an in-person interview, so the serious ones are already telling companies they'd rather just show up. A lot of companies paid good money to automate the handshake, and they're about to pay again to bring it back.
